title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Bell-Magendie law. Sensory roots carry information to the cord; motor roots carry commands to muscles.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Claude Bernard. Founder of experimental physiology; the internal environment, basis of homeostasis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: René Descartes. Mechanism and mind-body dualism; the soul meets the body at the pineal gland.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ancient Egypt. Embalming gave practical knowledge of the organs, but for religious and funerary purposes, not anatomical science.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Galen. Roman-era physician to gladiators; animal dissection, teleology, three spirits; his authority lasted for centuries.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Luigi Galvani. Electrical stimulation contracts frog muscle: the start of bioelectricity.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ancient Greece. Surface anatomy in sculpture, little human dissection; the Hippocratic theory of the four humours.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: William Harvey. Showed by experiment and calculation that blood circulates; the heart is a pump.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ibn al-Nafis. 13th-century Syrian physician who correctly described pulmonary circulation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Nuremberg Code. 1947: voluntary consent becomes essential in human experimentation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Andreas Vesalius. De humani corporis fabrica (1543) revolutionised anatomical teaching.

title: Why study the history of medicine?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Why study the history of medicine?
body.back: Humility, critical thinking, contextual understanding, ethical awareness and perspective; not to memorise dates.

title: Four dimensions of progress?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Four dimensions of progress?
body.back: Scientific, therapeutic, ethical, social; they do not advance at the same pace.

title: Harvey versus Descartes on the heart?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Harvey versus Descartes on the heart?
body.back: Harvey: a pump driving continuous circulation. Descartes: movement by heat and expansion of blood.

title: Comte's three stages?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Comte's three stages?
body.back: Theological, metaphysical, positive.

title: Claude Bernard?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Claude Bernard?
body.back: Experimental method (observe, hypothesise, identify, test); milieu intérieur → homeostasis.

title: Research ethics milestones?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Research ethics milestones?
body.back: Nuremberg Code 1947 (voluntary consent), Declaration of Helsinki 1964, PETA 1980.

title: Broca and Penfield?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Broca and Penfield?
body.back: Broca 1861: left frontal lobe and speech. Penfield: cortical maps by stimulation during surgery.

title: Three frameworks for illness?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Three frameworks for illness?
body.back: Balance and harmony; faith and divine will; evidence and technology. They often coexisted.

title: Galen: who, how, what idea?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Galen: who, how, what idea?
body.back: Physician to gladiators; mostly animal dissection; teleology; three spirits; authority for centuries.

title: Vesalius?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Vesalius?
body.back: De humani corporis fabrica, 1543: revolutionised anatomical teaching.

title: Auenbrugger and Laennec?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Auenbrugger and Laennec?
body.back: Percussion (1761) and auscultation: seeing inside the living body.

title: Burke and Hare?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Burke and Hare?
body.back: Murders in Edinburgh to sell bodies to Robert Knox → British Anatomy Act 1832.

title: The four humours and their elements?
subject: subj:history

body.front: The four humours and their elements?
body.back: Blood-air-warmth; phlegm-water-coldness; yellow bile-fire-dryness; black bile-earth-coldness.

title: Galen's three spirits?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Galen's three spirits?
body.back: Natural (liver, nutrition), vital (heart, heat and life), animal (brain, sensation and movement).

title: Who described pulmonary circulation before Harvey?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Who described pulmonary circulation before Harvey?
body.back: Ibn al-Nafis (13th century); Michael Servetus (1553, burned in Geneva).

title: List the stages of a society's reaction to an epidemic.
subject: subj:history

body.front: List the stages of a society's reaction to an epidemic.
body.back: Denial/delayed acceptance → panic, terror, chaos, flight → explanatory frameworks and perceived causes → control measures → resumption of normal life with new knowledge and prevention policies.

title: Black Death: date, impact, cause, control?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Black Death: date, impact, cause, control?
body.back: 1348 first wave from Asia; killed ~30% of Europe; Yersinia pestis, black rat host, flea vector (confirmed by DNA); quarantine, home confinement, plague doctors, pesthouses.

title: Syphilis and leprosy: what social lessons?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Syphilis and leprosy: what social lessons?
body.back: Syphilis ('French disease', 1490s, Treponema pallidum, penicillin) linked love and death and led to scandalous trials on prostitutes. Leprosy (M. leprae, Hansen) shows excessive stigma for a mildly contagious disease; WHO now fights discrimination.

title: Cholera: key dates?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Cholera: key dates?
body.back: Early 19th c. in Europe and North America; blamed on the poor and immigrants; John Snow linked it to drinking water in 1854; Vibrio cholerae identified in 1884; still spreads via sewage-contaminated water.

title: How was smallpox controlled and eradicated?
subject: subj:history

body.front: How was smallpox controlled and eradicated?
body.back: Two principles: it was inevitable and survivors were immune. Jenner 1798: cowpox protects against smallpox. Vaccination spread; eradicated 9 December 1979; two samples remain.

title: Tuberculosis in the 19th–20th century?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Tuberculosis in the 19th–20th century?
body.back: Main adult killer of the 19th c. (wasting, fever, cough); sanatoria; McKeown (1970) questioned whether medicine deserved credit for the mortality decline.

title: Influenza 1918 and AIDS: key facts?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Influenza 1918 and AIDS: key facts?
body.back: 1918 'Spanish flu' (not from Spain): 25–100 million deaths, new control institutions. AIDS: USA 1981, first 'GRID', millions of deaths (Africa), innocent/guilty victim narrative, delayed investigation, antiretrovirals but no eradication.

title: What was the Moroccan oil tragedy?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What was the Moroccan oil tragedy?
body.back: 1959: acute epidemic of paralysis of all four limbs affecting whole families, in Meknes then the Rif and other regions of Morocco.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: AIDS. USA 1981, first called GRID; innocent/guilty victims; antiretrovirals.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cholera. Blamed on the poor; John Snow linked it to water in 1854; Vibrio cholerae 1884.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: COVID-19. Compare with past pandemics and their lessons.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Influenza 1918. The 'Spanish flu': 25 to 100 million deaths; new control institutions.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Moroccan oil tragedy. 1959 epidemic of four-limb paralysis, Meknes then the Rif.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Black Death. 1348, 30% of Europe; Yersinia pestis via the black rat's flea; quarantine born.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Smallpox. Jenner's cowpox experiment 1798; eradicated 9 December 1979.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Syphilis. The 'French disease' of the 1490s; sexually transmitted; penicillin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Tuberculosis. Main adult killer of the 19th century; sanatoria; McKeown 1970.

title: What consequences do epidemics have?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What consequences do epidemics have?
body.back: Economic (trade, labour), social (flight, stigma), intellectual (explanations, science) and political (institutions, policies).

title: Explanations offered for the Black Death?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Explanations offered for the Black Death?
body.back: Atmospheric alterations and constellations; divine punishment for corrupt priests; blame on travellers, strangers and minorities.

title: Clinical picture of bubonic plague?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Clinical picture of bubonic plague?
body.back: Fever, swollen lymph nodes (buboes), dehydration and death.

title: Syphilis in history?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Syphilis in history?
body.back: 'French disease' after the 1490s outbreak in French armies; painful skin lesions; recognised as sexual (first lesions genital); love and death; scandalous trials on prostitutes.

title: Leprosy today?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Leprosy today?
body.back: Still present in many regions; Hansen's disease (M. leprae); WHO strategy 2016–2020 built on anti-discrimination.

title: Cholera: clinical picture and social response?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Cholera: clinical picture and social response?
body.back: Massive diarrhoea and quick death; blamed on the poor and immigrants; sick newcomers confined with healthy ones in unsanitary settings.

title: Smallpox: history in five points?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Smallpox: history in five points?
body.back: Endemic since antiquity; killed kings and peasants; biological weapon (blankets); controlled by inevitability/immunity principles; Jenner 1798; eradicated 1979.

title: AIDS: key features of the epidemic?
subject: subj:history

body.front: AIDS: key features of the epidemic?
body.back: 1981 USA, homosexual men, 'GRID'; millions of deaths especially in Africa; innocent vs guilty victims; delayed credibility; questionable measures; antiretrovirals without eradication.

title: Questions the lecture asks about COVID-19?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Questions the lecture asks about COVID-19?
body.back: What do you know about it; similarities with the plague; lessons learnt on control and prevention; how it affected our lives and whether it was all bad.

title: Other global epidemics listed?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Other global epidemics listed?
body.back: Ebola (1990s), bilharzia (1970s), mad cow disease (2001), swine influenza (2009), and the Moroccan oil tragedy (1959).

title: Facial cues of contempt, disgust and surprise?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Facial cues of contempt, disgust and surprise?
body.back: Contempt: one raised brow, sideways glance, curled lip, head tilted back. Disgust: wrinkled nose bridge, lowered brows, curled upper lip. Surprise: wide eyes, dilated pupils, arched brows, open mouth.

title: Facial cues of fear, anger and sadness?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Facial cues of fear, anger and sadness?
body.back: Fear: wide eyes, raised/furrowed brows, tense mouth, pallor. Anger: narrowed eyes, furrowed brows, clenched jaw, pressed lips/bared teeth. Sadness: pained brows, drooping lids, watery eyes, downturned mouth.

title: Five keys to emotional intelligence and the components of self-awareness?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Five keys to emotional intelligence and the components of self-awareness?
body.back: Self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills. Self-awareness: social style, personality, emotions, values/motivation, mindset.

title: Short-term vs long-term self-regulation tools?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Short-term vs long-term self-regulation tools?
body.back: Short-term: mindfulness, conscious breathing, postural change, cognitive break, cognitive assessment, sensory grounding, positive self-talk. Long-term: proactive thinking, emotional journaling, emotional hygiene, positive visual image, cognitive empathy, self-compassion.

title: Three dimensions of empathy?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Three dimensions of empathy?
body.back: Cognitive (perspective-taking: understanding what the other thinks), emotional (standing in their shoes: feeling what they feel), behavioural (compassion: willingness to act to help).

title: Give an example of an empathic response to a friend criticised by a professor.
subject: subj:history

body.front: Give an example of an empathic response to a friend criticised by a professor.
body.back: 'That sounds like a tough experience; anyone would feel discouraged after feedback delivered that way. If you want to talk it through, I'm here — maybe we can look at what was useful and plan tomorrow.'

title: Rules for the art of disagreeing?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Rules for the art of disagreeing?
body.back: It's OK to disagree, with grace: don't try to convince them you are right; try to understand how they feel; treat their feelings as information to process.

title: Four steps of non-violent communication, with an example?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Four steps of non-violent communication, with an example?
body.back: Observation ('when I was talking and you looked at your phone'), feeling ('I felt frustrated and unheard'), need ('because I need to feel listened to'), request ('would you put your phone aside for 10 minutes?').

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: The human side of care. Emotional intelligence in the service of patients and colleagues.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Conflict resolution. Thomas-Kilmann: balancing own interests with cooperation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Empathy. Perspective-taking, standing in someone's shoes, compassion.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Non-violent communication. Observation → feeling → need → request.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Observation. Attention with intention: reading confusion, fear, anger, sadness, contempt, disgust, surprise.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Self-awareness. Social style, personality, emotions, values, mindset.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Self-regulation. Short-term tools (breathing, grounding) and long-term tools (journaling, self-compassion).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Social skills. Active listening, the art of disagreeing, praising.

title: Cues of confusion and of surprise?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Cues of confusion and of surprise?
body.back: Confusion: eyebrows raised/drawn with forehead creases, narrowed unfocused eyes, mouth partly open, head tilted. Surprise: wide eyes, dilated pupils, arched brows, open mouth.

title: Cues of confidence and of disappointment?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Cues of confidence and of disappointment?
body.back: Confidence: relaxed steady eyes, slightly raised brows, small closed-lip smile, chin lifted. Disappointment: downcast half-closed eyes, lowered brows, slack downturned lips.

title: What does 'seeing beyond appearances' mean?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What does 'seeing beyond appearances' mean?
body.back: Expressions can conceal as much as they reveal; empathy expands perception; observation is attention with intention.

title: Components of self-awareness?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Components of self-awareness?
body.back: Social style (pragmatic vs humanistic), personality, emotions, values/motivation, mindset (toward personalities, stress, emotions, relationships).

title: The two personality scenarios in the lecture?
subject: subj:history

body.front: The two personality scenarios in the lecture?
body.back: Group study invitation before S5 exams: accept as a new experience or decline knowing yourself. Night before semiology exam: panic and skim, or a calm structured review then sleep.

title: Define emotional self-regulation.
subject: subj:history

body.front: Define emotional self-regulation.
body.back: Empowering thoughtful acting over reacting, with short-term (mindfulness, breathing, posture, cognitive break/assessment, grounding, positive self-talk) and long-term tools (proactive thinking, journaling, emotional hygiene, imagery, cognitive empathy, self-compassion).

title: Examples of rephrased self-talk?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Examples of rephrased self-talk?
body.back: 'I made an honest mistake; frustrating but fixable.' 'I need to refocus and ask for help.' 'My ideas aren't always chosen; get feedback.' 'He may not want a friendship, and that's OK.'

title: Empathic responses to an overwhelmed classmate?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Empathic responses to an overwhelmed classmate?
body.back: 'It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now; that must feel overwhelming.' 'Let's look at what's stressing you most and break it down together.'

title: What are the social skills listed?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What are the social skills listed?
body.back: Active listening, the art of disagreeing, praising, conflict resolution (Thomas-Kilmann), non-violent communication.

title: Write an NVC message for a friend who checks their phone while you talk.
subject: subj:history

body.front: Write an NVC message for a friend who checks their phone while you talk.
body.back: Observation: 'When I was talking and you looked at your phone.' Feeling: 'I felt frustrated and unheard.' Need: 'I need to feel listened to.' Request: 'Would you put your phone aside for 10 minutes?'

title: What are the five universal functions of pathology?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What are the five universal functions of pathology?
body.back: Explain suffering; identify the ailment (diagnosis); predict outcomes (prognosis); justify treatment; prove or refute an explanation (autopsy, forensic pathology).

title: Illness vs disease?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Illness vs disease?
body.back: Illness: individual suffering, constant in time and space, patient-centred. Disease: the medical theory about illness, changing with knowledge, involving patient, observer and illness.

title: Physiological vs ontological theories of disease?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Physiological vs ontological theories of disease?
body.back: Physiological: the inside, what the patient is (humoral imbalance, constitution). Ontological: the outside, what the patient has (supernatural agents, germs).

title: How did Greco-Roman antiquity change pathology?
subject: subj:history

body.front: How did Greco-Roman antiquity change pathology?
body.back: Refuted supernatural causes; disease as natural imbalance of four elements/humours; Hippocratic observation and reasoning (e.g. The Sacred Disease — epilepsy has a natural cause); treatment by restoring balance (bleeding, diet, baths).

title: Key figures in nosology?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Key figures in nosology?
body.back: Rhazes (9th c.): fevers with and without rash. Sydenham (UK): gout and dropsy, observation over theory. Renaissance: decline of Galenism, iatrophysics/iatrochemistry, uroscopy.

title: Why was anatomy long irrelevant to bedside medicine, and what changed?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Why was anatomy long irrelevant to bedside medicine, and what changed?
body.back: Changes were hidden until death, might be due to death, and could not be repaired. Morgagni (1761) correlated diseases with lesions; 19th-century physical diagnosis linked symptoms to anatomy; the microscope (1830s) and Virchow's cell theory made diagnosis rest on findings.

title: Name the three founders of germ theory and their contributions.
subject: subj:history

body.front: Name the three founders of germ theory and their contributions.
body.back: Pasteur (French chemist): bacteria cause disease, vaccines. Lister (British surgeon): carbolic-acid antisepsis. Koch (German physician): Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Nobel 1905.

title: What does 'heredity strikes back' refer to?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What does 'heredity strikes back' refer to?
body.back: After the germ era, the ancient concept of heredity returned: cells → chromosomes → DNA (Watson & Crick 1952, Nobel 1962) → molecular pathology, molecular cancer types, paleopathology.

title: What is the current pathology model and its risk?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is the current pathology model and its risk?
body.back: A blend of internal (physiological) and external (ontological) factors, with epigenetics linking both. Risk: extrapolation that blames patients or stigmatises communities.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pathology at the bedside. Greco-Roman humoral imbalance, Hippocratic observation, nosology of symptoms.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Current model. Physiological and ontological causes blended by epigenetics.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Disease. The changing medical idea about illness, involving patient, observer and illness.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Five functions of pathology. Explain suffering, identify (diagnosis), predict (prognosis), justify treatment, prove or refute.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Heredity strikes back. DNA in 1952, molecular pathology, paleopathology.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Illness. The patient's individual suffering, constant in time and space.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pathology moves to the morgue. Morgagni's autopsy correlations, the microscope and Virchow, then germ theory.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Supernatural causes. Illness as punishment or test from higher powers; treatment by restoring faith.

title: Explain the function 'explain suffering'.
subject: subj:history

body.front: Explain the function 'explain suffering'.
body.back: Giving a logical account of illness through cultural/spiritual beliefs (sin, blame) or scientific grounds (structure, function, heredity, contagion).

title: Explain the function 'identify the ailment'.
subject: subj:history

body.front: Explain the function 'identify the ailment'.
body.back: Diagnosis: the clinician collects symptoms and signs; observation plus knowledge labels the ailment; defining the abnormal also defines the normal, which keeps changing.

title: Explain 'predict outcomes' and 'justify treatment'.
subject: subj:history

body.front: Explain 'predict outcomes' and 'justify treatment'.
body.back: Prognosis moved from divination to statistics; therapeutic rationales are applied post hoc and change while remedies persist.

title: Explain 'prove or refute an explanation'.
subject: subj:history

body.front: Explain 'prove or refute an explanation'.
body.back: Autopsies for retrospective diagnosis since the 13th century, widespread in medicine and law since the 19th (forensic pathology, malpractice).

title: Supernatural causes: features?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Supernatural causes: features?
body.back: Ontological origin from higher powers to punish or test; illness features unimportant, patient's idea of cause central; treatment restores integrity and faith.

title: How does religion still shape illness today?
subject: subj:history

body.front: How does religion still shape illness today?
body.back: It comforts sufferers, but some illnesses are seen as deserved (AIDS, addiction), health as superiority, chronic illness as trial.

title: Hippocratic treatment of humoral imbalance?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Hippocratic treatment of humoral imbalance?
body.back: Restore balance: bleeding, diet, baths, fumigation; physiological theory except trauma and miasma; Galen's eclectic vitalism prevailed.

title: Renaissance changes in bedside pathology?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Renaissance changes in bedside pathology?
body.back: Decline of Galenism, rise of sensualism (iatrophysics, iatrochemistry), uroscopy as a diagnostic tool, nosology as a system.

title: Sequence of the morgue era?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Sequence of the morgue era?
body.back: Morgagni 1761 (autopsy correlations) → 19th-century physical diagnosis (symptoms linked to lesions) → 1830s microscope, Virchow → 1880s germ theory and hospital labs.

title: Why did the germ era shadow heredity, and how did heredity return?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Why did the germ era shadow heredity, and how did heredity return?
body.back: External invaders explained infections spectacularly; but bacteriology → microscopes → cells → chromosomes → DNA (1952) revived internal causes: molecular pathology, molecular cancer types.

title: How were most therapies discovered, and what is the main confounder?
subject: subj:history

body.front: How were most therapies discovered, and what is the main confounder?
body.back: Empirically — observation, accident, trial and error — with the placebo effect as the main problem.

title: The two historical rationales for treatment?
subject: subj:history

body.front: The two historical rationales for treatment?
body.back: Similia similibus curantur (like cures like → homeopathy, restoration of health) and contraria contrariis curantur (opposite cures opposite → healing with side effects).

title: What were Mithridate and Theriac?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What were Mithridate and Theriac?
body.back: Poison antidotes: Mithridate (1st century BC) and Theriac (therion = beast), used with a mystical aura until the 19th century.

title: What marked the 15th-century 'advent of metals'?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What marked the 15th-century 'advent of metals'?
body.back: Alchemist influence; minerals with healing effects — copper, sulphur, salt, mercury; mercury for syphilis, antimony for everything.

title: Who were the apothecaries?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Who were the apothecaries?
body.back: Early pharmacists who made and dispensed materia medica, mostly women; botany was a core medical subject until the 20th century (botanical gardens like Chelsea Physic Garden).

title: Tell the story of insulin in three lines.
subject: subj:history

body.front: Tell the story of insulin in three lines.
body.back: 1922, Toronto General Hospital: Banting and Best under Macleod, purified by Collip, injected diabetic children in coma who awoke. Patent sold to the university for $1. Nobel Prize 1923 to Banting and Macleod.

title: Timeline of the clinical trial?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Timeline of the clinical trial?
body.back: Lind 1747 (scurvy); formalised early 19th c. with statistics; untreated controls 1900s; committees 1930s; randomisation 1940s; blinding/standardisation after 1940; Nuremberg Code 1947 → evidence-based medicine.

title: What does 'magic bullets → magic problems' refer to?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What does 'magic bullets → magic problems' refer to?
body.back: Drug resistance, nosocomial infections, dangerous side effects, doubt that drugs alone raised life expectancy, and disillusionment with universal eradication.

title: Thalidomide: what happened and who is the hero?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Thalidomide: what happened and who is the hero?
body.back: About 10,000 children harmed in 25 countries; Frances Oldham Kelsey (1962) blocked US approval, vindicating careful licensing.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antibiotics. After germ theory: Fleming's penicillin, widespread by 1945.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Apothecaries. Early pharmacists, mostly women; botany taught until the 20th century.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Evidence-based medicine. The outcome of formalised trials.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Galenical pharmacology. Balance of humours, about 300 medications, mithridate and theriac.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Insulin. Banting, Best, Macleod and Collip; children woke from coma; patent sold for one dollar.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mysticism and magic. Early remedies; 'like cures like' and 'opposite cures opposite'.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Advent of metals. 15th century: copper, sulphur, salt, mercury; mercury for syphilis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Thalidomide. About 10,000 children harmed; Frances Oldham Kelsey blocked US approval.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Clinical trials. Lind 1747; controls, committees, randomisation, blinding, ethics.

title: Why is the placebo effect a problem for empirical pharmacology?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Why is the placebo effect a problem for empirical pharmacology?
body.back: Because remedies found by observation and trial-and-error may seem to work when improvement comes from expectation, not the drug — hence the need for controls and blinding.

title: Like vs opposite in one table?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Like vs opposite in one table?
body.back: Like (similia): restoration of health, homeopathy. Opposite (contraria): healing, side effects.

title: Galenical pharmacology?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Galenical pharmacology?
body.back: Re-establish humoral balance; non-drug remedies; about 300 internal/external medications; mithridate/theriac with mystical aura until the 19th century; healing power of nature; first do no harm.

title: Classification of drugs through history?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Classification of drugs through history?
body.back: Poison vs antidote; physical properties (solids, liquids); physiological effect (laxatives, emetics, narcotics); pure drugs vs complex mixtures after the French Revolution.

title: Magic bullets: two families?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Magic bullets: two families?
body.back: Antibiotics (Fleming, penicillin, 1945) after germ theory; hormones replacing deficiencies (insulin 1922).

title: Who did what for insulin?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Who did what for insulin?
body.back: Banting and Best did the experiments under Macleod at Toronto; Collip purified; patent sold to the university for $1; Nobel 1923 to Banting and Macleod.

title: What did James Lind do in 1747?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What did James Lind do in 1747?
body.back: Ran a comparative trial of treatments for scurvy in sailors — the prototype clinical trial.

title: Steps toward evidence-based medicine?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Steps toward evidence-based medicine?
body.back: Early 19th c. statistics; 1900s controls; 1930s committees; 1940s randomisation; after 1940 blinding/standardisation; 1947 Nuremberg ethics.

title: What are 'magic problems'?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What are 'magic problems'?
body.back: Drug resistance, nosocomial infections, dangerous side effects, doubt about drugs' role in longevity, disillusionment with universal eradication.

title: Thalidomide in two lines?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Thalidomide in two lines?
body.back: A sedative causing severe birth defects in about 10,000 children in 25 countries; Frances Oldham Kelsey (FDA, 1962) refused approval, vindicating careful licensing.

title: What are the three dualisms that run through the history of physiology?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What are the three dualisms that run through the history of physiology?
body.back: Concept of life: vitalism vs mechanism. Method of inquiry: teleology vs empiricism. Study strategy: speculation vs experimentation.

title: Summarise Galen's physiology.
subject: subj:history

body.front: Summarise Galen's physiology.
body.back: Balance of four humours; three spirits (natural in liver, vital in lungs, animal in brain); blood made in the liver flowing outward from the heart through imaginary pores; teleological faculties for each organ.

title: Who challenged Galen on circulation, and when?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Who challenged Galen on circulation, and when?
body.back: Ibn al-Nafis (13th c., pulmonary circulation, unknown in Europe), Michael Servetus (burned 1553), William Harvey (17th c., heart as pump, blood circulates — start of experimental physiology).

title: Descartes' contribution to physiology?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Descartes' contribution to physiology?
body.back: Mind-body dualism; life explained by mechanical laws (iatromechanism, human as a clock); animal spirits as particles in nerves; soul only human, in the pineal gland.

title: What did iatrochemistry propose, and who demonstrated it?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What did iatrochemistry propose, and who demonstrated it?
body.back: Life is combustion. John Mayow's candle and mouse: only some air sustains burning and life — breathable air = burnable air; life as combustion of carbon with oxygen.

title: Key 19th-century physiology discoveries and names?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Key 19th-century physiology discoveries and names?
body.back: Legallois: respiratory centre in the medulla. Bell-Magendie law: motor vs sensory nerves. Magendie: Journal de physiologie (1821). Claude Bernard: milieu intérieur, experimental method. Beaumont: gastric fistula studies.

title: Claude Bernard's experimental approach in one sentence?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Claude Bernard's experimental approach in one sentence?
body.back: Observe a phenomenon, localise it to an anatomical structure, then surgically alter that structure to study the effects — guided by doubt.

title: List the main points of the Nuremberg Code (1947).
subject: subj:history

body.front: List the main points of the Nuremberg Code (1947).
body.back: Voluntary informed consent; useful results for society; based on prior knowledge; avoid unnecessary suffering; no expected death/disability; risk proportional to importance; proper facilities; qualified researchers; right to withdraw; stop if harm appears.

title: 20th-century milestones in physiology?
subject: subj:history

body.front: 20th-century milestones in physiology?
body.back: First Nobel Prize (1901); physiology in medical education (Osler); life reduced to physicochemical terms; psychiatry/psychology physiological from the 1950s; Nuremberg Code 1947, Helsinki 1968, PETA 1980; specialisation (neurosciences).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Claude Bernard. Experimental method and the constant milieu intérieur.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: René Descartes. Mind-body dualism; the body as a clock; soul in the pineal gland.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Galen. Four humours, three spirits, blood flowing outward through pores in the heart.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Luigi Galvani. Animal electricity: current produces a reflex movement.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: William Harvey. Showed blood circulates and the heart is a pump: the start of experimental physiology.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: François Magendie. Journal de physiologie, 1821; Bell-Magendie law.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: John Mayow. Candle and mouse: breathable air equals burnable air; life as combustion.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ibn al-Nafis. Described the pulmonary circulation in the 13th century, unknown in Europe until translated.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Nuremberg Code. 1947 rules for human experimentation, starting with informed consent.

title: Vitalism vs mechanism?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Vitalism vs mechanism?
body.back: Vitalism: peculiar life forces, not reducible to physics, tied to spirit/soul. Mechanism: physical and chemical forces; materialism (existence = tangible matter).

title: Teleology vs empiricism, speculation vs experimentation?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Teleology vs empiricism, speculation vs experimentation?
body.back: Teleology: doctrine of causes and purpose, meaning of life. Empiricism: knowledge by pure observation. Speculation: armchair reasoning. Experimentation: recent experimental methods.

title: Physiology in antiquity?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Physiology in antiquity?
body.back: Four elements, four humours in balance; three spirits (natural/liver, vital/lungs, animal/brain); Galen's outward blood flow with heart pores and organ faculties.

title: Medieval physiology?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Medieval physiology?
body.back: Galen repeated with fascination; doubts unexpressed before the 15th–16th centuries; Ibn al-Nafis described pulmonary circulation (13th c.); Servetus burned in 1553.

title: Harvey's argument?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Harvey's argument?
body.back: Blood circulates through lungs and body and is not constantly renewed; the heart is a pump — proven by mathematics and experiment; first serious challenge to Galen.

title: Iatromechanism vs iatrochemistry?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Iatromechanism vs iatrochemistry?
body.back: Iatromechanism (Descartes): body as a clock, similarities with mechanics. Iatrochemistry (Mayow): life as combustion; candle and mouse experiment.

title: 19th-century discoveries?
subject: subj:history

body.front: 19th-century discoveries?
body.back: Respiratory centre in the medulla (Legallois), Bell-Magendie law (motor/sensory nerves), Magendie's journal 1821, Bernard's milieu intérieur and surgical-alteration method, Beaumont's gastric fistula.

title: Human research subjects in history?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Human research subjects in history?
body.back: Survivors of accidents and diseases, researchers (Santorio) and student volunteers, disadvantaged people (condemned criminals, soldiers, prostitutes, racial minorities), Nazi prisoners.

title: Ethics milestones?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Ethics milestones?
body.back: Nuremberg Code 1947, Declaration of Helsinki 1968, PETA 1980.

title: What did 20th-century physiology achieve?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What did 20th-century physiology achieve?
body.back: Closer link with medicine; first Nobel Prize 1901; physiology in medical education (Osler); reduction of life to physicochemical terms; physiological psychiatry/psychology; specialisation.

title: Medicine vs surgery, historically?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Medicine vs surgery, historically?
body.back: Medicine: science, wisdom, work of the mind, university physicians reading Greek. Surgery: technical skill, work of the hand, barber-class apprenticeship. Professionalised via Royal Colleges (physicians 1518, surgeons 1843).

title: Evidence of prehistoric and ancient surgery?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Evidence of prehistoric and ancient surgery?
body.back: Trephinated skulls (10,000 BC), Tafoughalt mandibular surgery (12,000 BC), splints (2400 BC), army-ant sutures, Babylonian malpractice code, Edwin Smith Papyrus (1600 BC, 48 cases), Egyptian mummification sutures.

title: Who dominated medieval surgery and who is the father of modern surgery?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Who dominated medieval surgery and who is the father of modern surgery?
body.back: Al-Zahrawi (Abulcasis), translated into Latin — bloodletting, cautery, instruments. Ambroise Paré (1510–1590): 'I bandage them but God heals them'.

title: How was pain conquered?
subject: subj:history

body.front: How was pain conquered?
body.back: Before: alcohol, opium and bleeding to induce fainting. Ether (1840s) — word 'anaesthesia'; chloroform 1845. Deaths on the table and post-operative complications persisted.

title: How was infection conquered?
subject: subj:history

body.front: How was infection conquered?
body.back: Semmelweis 1847 (hand-washing with chlorinated lime), Lister 1867 (carbolic acid on open fractures), rubber gloves 1878 — asepsis preferred over antisepsis.

title: Firsts of the surgical century (1870–1970)?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Firsts of the surgical century (1870–1970)?
body.back: Gall bladder 1867; appendicitis described 1889 (McBurney); Kocher Nobel 1909; open heart 1952 (Lillehei); kidney transplant 1954 (Murray, Nobel 1990); heart transplant 1967 (Barnard); plastic surgery from wars; laparoscopy, microsurgery, laser.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anaesthesia. Ether in the 1840s gave the word; chloroform 1845.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Antisepsis and asepsis. Semmelweis 1847, Lister 1867, rubber gloves 1878.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Babylonian code. Malpractice law: hands cut off for harming a free man.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Edwin Smith Papyrus. Egyptian surgical treatise, 48 case reports, interpreted 1930.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Surgical optimism. 1870–1970: gall bladder 1867, appendicitis 1889, Kocher Nobel 1909.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ambroise Paré. 1510–1590, father of surgery: 'I bandage them but God heals them'.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Prehistoric surgery. Trephinated skulls and mandibular surgery in Morocco's Pigeons' cave.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transplantation. Kidney 1954 (Murray), heart 1967 (Barnard).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Al-Zahrawi (Abulcasis). Dominated medieval surgery: bloodletting, cautery, instruments.

title: Medicine vs surgery in the lecture's contrast?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Medicine vs surgery in the lecture's contrast?
body.back: Medicine: science, wisdom, work of the mind. Surgery: technical, skills, work of the hand.

title: How did warfare shape surgery?
subject: subj:history

body.front: How did warfare shape surgery?
body.back: Dangerous survival techniques → safer compensatory techniques → peacetime applications; urgent surgery (necessity) then elective surgery (intention).

title: The Babylonian code on surgery?
subject: subj:history

body.front: The Babylonian code on surgery?
body.back: If a surgeon harms a free man's slave, he replaces the slave; if he hurts a free man, his hands are cut off (stele at the Louvre).

title: The Edwin Smith Papyrus?
subject: subj:history

body.front: The Edwin Smith Papyrus?
body.back: 1600 BC Egyptian surgical treatise, 48 case reports with diagnosis and management; New York Academy of Medicine; interpreted 1930.

title: Physician vs surgeon before professionalisation?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Physician vs surgeon before professionalisation?
body.back: Physician: scientist reading Greek, university, first patients after graduating. Surgeon: barber class, often illiterate, apprenticeship, learning by doing.

title: Milestones of professionalisation?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Milestones of professionalisation?
body.back: Royal College of Physicians 1518, Royal College of Surgeons of England 1843; French surgeons' rise with the Napoleonic wars.

title: Anaesthesia and its problems?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Anaesthesia and its problems?
body.back: Ether 1840s (the word 'anaesthesia'), chloroform 1845; deaths on the table and post-operative complications remained.

title: Antisepsis vs asepsis?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Antisepsis vs asepsis?
body.back: Antisepsis kills germs on wounds (Lister's carbolic acid 1867, Semmelweis's chlorinated lime 1847); asepsis prevents contamination (rubber gloves 1878), and became preferred.

title: List the surgical firsts 1867–1967.
subject: subj:history

body.front: List the surgical firsts 1867–1967.
body.back: Gall bladder 1867; appendicitis described 1889 (McBurney); Kocher Nobel 1909; open heart 1952 (Lillehei); kidney transplant 1954 (Murray); heart transplant 1967 (Barnard).

title: Current surgical polemics?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Current surgical polemics?
body.back: Cost-effectiveness of expensive procedures; plastic/aesthetic surgery versus medical necessity.

title: Tell the story of the stethoscope.
subject: subj:history

body.front: Tell the story of the stethoscope.
body.back: 1816: Laennec, restrained by decorum from direct auscultation of a lady, rolled a notebook into a cylinder and heard the heart. He described lung and heart sounds; first internationally popular diagnostic instrument; anatomical change detectable in the living; died of TB at 45.

title: Key microscope milestones?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Key microscope milestones?
body.back: Van Leeuwenhoek 1670 (microscopic pathology); Ramón y Cajal — synapses, neuron theory, Nobel 1906; electron microscope 1931 by Ruska (Nobel 1986), reaching the molecular level.

title: Imaging milestones?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Imaging milestones?
body.back: Photography 1820s (pathology teaching, chronophotography of movement); Röntgen's X-rays 1895 (Nobel 1901); then ultrasound, CT scan, MRI.

title: What was the Asilomar conference?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What was the Asilomar conference?
body.back: 1975: 140 biologists, physicians, lawyers and science writers agreeing on responsible use of recombinant DNA — bacteria making human proteins, diagnosis and therapy, later stem cells and bioethics.

title: What are the consequences of medical technology on the concept of disease?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What are the consequences of medical technology on the concept of disease?
body.back: Huge diagnostic and therapeutic benefits; a revolution in the concept of disease (hypertension defined by measurement); paradoxes and side effects; the shifting definition of normality.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Asilomar conference. 1975: responsible use of recombinant DNA.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Neuron theory. Ramón y Cajal described synapses; Nobel 1906.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Electron microscope. Ruska 1931, Nobel 1986; vision to the molecular level.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Modern imaging. Ultrasound, CT scan and MRI.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: The microscope. Van Leeuwenhoek 1670: microscopic pathology begins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: What is normality?. Technology revolutionised the concept of disease, e.g. hypertension.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Photography. 1820s: used in teaching pathology and studying movement.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: The stethoscope. Laennec 1816: first internationally popular diagnostic instrument.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: X-rays. Röntgen 1895, Nobel 1901; the root of modern imaging.

title: Who was Laennec and what were his values?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Who was Laennec and what were his values?
body.back: René Laennec (1781–1826), a physician concerned with modesty and hygiene; invented the stethoscope in 1816 out of decorum.

title: Impact of the stethoscope?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Impact of the stethoscope?
body.back: Detailed lung and heart sound descriptions; first internationally popular diagnostic instrument; anatomical change detectable in the living; changed the concept of disease.

title: Laennec's warning to colleagues?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Laennec's warning to colleagues?
body.back: Do not rely too heavily on organic explanations: doctors listen not only to patients' chests but to their stories.

title: From light to electron microscope?
subject: subj:history

body.front: From light to electron microscope?
body.back: Van Leeuwenhoek 1670 (tissues, pathology); Cajal's synapses/neuron theory (Nobel 1906); Ruska's electron microscope 1931 (Nobel 1986), molecules and cell function.

title: Uses of photography in medicine?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Uses of photography in medicine?
body.back: Teaching pathology extensively; study of movement through chronophotography.

title: Röntgen's discovery and its descendants?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Röntgen's discovery and its descendants?
body.back: X-rays 1895 (Nobel 1901); rapid spread; today ultrasound, CT and MRI.

title: What happened at Asilomar in 1975?
subject: subj:history

body.front: What happened at Asilomar in 1975?
body.back: 140 biologists, physicians, lawyers and science writers set rules for responsible use of recombinant DNA.

title: Consequences of technology in four points?
subject: subj:history

body.front: Consequences of technology in four points?
body.back: Benefits in diagnosis/treatment; revolution in the concept of disease (hypertension); paradoxes and side effects; the question of normality.
